web_evidence.title: Book of the Dead by Patricia Cornwell | Excerpt
web_evidence.note: The sustained Rome opening externally narrates both victim and killer as she/he and enters the killer's memories and perceptions without a participating narrator.

web_evidence.title: Excerpt: 'Book of the Dead'
web_evidence.note: The opened Chapter 1 excerpt sustains third-person narration around Kay Scarpetta, Benton Wesley, and Italian investigators, including Scarpetta's knowledge and reactions.

web_evidence.title: Crime Novelist Patricia Cornwell on Blood, 'Boundaries' and Her Next Book
web_evidence.note: ABC explicitly identifies Book of the Dead as replacing Scarpetta's first-person narration with omniscient third person that can expose the perpetrator's thoughts.

web_evidence.title: Book of the Dead by Patricia D. Cornwell
web_evidence.note: Publishers Weekly describes Cornwell's switch from first- to third-person narration and notes shifts among viewpoints, corroborating a multifocal third-person structure rather than alternating grammatical persons.

web_evidence.title: Patricia Cornwell Interview
web_evidence.note: In the interview, Cornwell herself identifies Book of the Dead as one of the books in which she went to third-person point of view.

person_note: The diagnostic Goodreads passages repeatedly show a nonparticipating narrator presenting Scarpetta, Lucy, and other focal characters externally while also accessing their perceptions and histories. First- and second-person forms in the remaining quotes are dialogue or generic aphorisms, not competing base narration. Two sustained web excerpts independently show third-person narration, and several credible whole-book descriptions—including Cornwell's own account—identify the novel's structure as third-person and omniscient or multifocal. The web excerpts themselves cover only the opening and Chapter 1, but the whole-book structural sources and varied interior quote passages resolve that scope limitation; no credible contrary person evidence was found.
